utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we resume the examination-in-chief, two small technical matters. First of all we discussed yesterday the -- I would say the easy accessible storage of exhibits. I hope I was not over optimistic when I said it should not be too difficult to get them on -- in an easy, accessible way, just as the Judges -- by the way, by doing the work, themselves, and within the team, got them from the judicial database where they are accessible but less easy accessible compared to where we put them now, just in a folder on our computers. We are still working on it to see whether not the accessibility but the easy accessibility could be made available to the parties as well. That's point one. I can't give you any promise but it has my attention and we are looking at it. It's altogether three gigabytes so we hope we can handle it but it's certainly not to be done just by one CD. It's far more. Second. I did understand that sometimes if a B/C/S copy fails on our easy, accessible folder, Mr. Registrar is friendly enough to then provide me as an annex through an e-mail that B/C/S original so that I can consult it on my computer. I do understand that if he does that, he sends at the same time a copy to the Defence as well. So it's just a matter of opening the attachment to your e-mail that arrives at that very same moment and it's available for the parties. You may understand that we are trying to accommodate to the extent possible, practically possible, because we would not, for example, do for the Defence or the Prosecution again the work if it could not be copied right away, to take it from the judicial database, copy it into a special folder, because that is time-consuming and takes overtime from our staff. Second issue, Mr. Krajisnik, you have provided Mr. Registrar with an electronic copy of some of the documents we discussed yesterday, among them the blue map, also to make it available to the Defence once the formalities are fulfilled you'll receive the CD-ROM on which these documents appear. These are the practical matters I would like to -- not to discuss but at least to announce at this very moment. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I did ask for the opportunity just to raise a couple of points on that area for this reason that sometimes Your Honour we spend a few minutes in court but actually a great deal of sometimes has to be spent out of court as the alternative in communicating A with B, B with C, and so on. So sometimes it's easier to deal with it when everybody is here and listening at the same time. Your Honour is absolutely right about the difficulties of the JDB. I'm not quite clear. I hadn't understood that the material went from the JDB to the Trial Chamber. I thought it might be the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We copy it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. So when it goes from somewhere then on to the JDB is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the Registry at this moment -- the Registry is responsible for, I would say, filling the JDB and they are doing their utmost best to have everything on the judicial database but have not completed. We are thinking in terms of, for exhibits I think it's 80 per cent by now or even more. So most of the exhibits are on the judicial database, and once they are there we copy them in such a way to our own computers that they are easy accessible. I wouldn't say that the judicial database is not easy accessible but not as easy as just having them in one folder under the exhibit number on your own PC, which takes me approximately five seconds to get them on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the -- I think we probably all appreciate that the JDB, the problem is it takes to locate a document and then download it on to one's own hard disk takes a couple of minutes or so per document, and if there are thousands of documents obviously that's an awful lot of personnel. So that's the reason that's not practical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In our team they do it more quickly. First of all it's not thousands of documents but exhibits is approximately 11, 1200.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With due respect, Your Honour, it is thousands because some of the exhibits themselves contain very large numbers of documents. It is thousands of documents. Your Honour, with respect, that's an indisputable fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you copy a file, not a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I'm lost here, Your Honour. The individual documents are on individual files but Your Honour we are debating something futile here. It's an awful lot of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That work has been done and if possible it will be made available to you. If not possible, unfortunately, you'll have to do the same as we had to do, that is to copy it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, that's really my point, Your Honour. That would, with respect that would be absurd, that we end up with my team or anybody's team having to do that work all over again. I entirely accept Your Honour's point that there is also no reason why lots of overtime should be done to service us but Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I asked yesterday the one's who did it and said it took me several hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To do what, with respect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To do the copying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the documents from the judicial database to their own computers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know what to say, Your Honour. I speak to my team who belong to the same human race as Your Honour's team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are trying to do our utmost best. You say it's a problem. Okay, let's just assume that we could not achieve that. What would then be your comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to get -- I do have some technical knowledge of this, Your Honour, but I'm trying to get, with respect, just a little bit to the bottom of it. It appears that the Registry, the first stage of the process, the Registry have the material in some usable, accessible form, before it goes on the judicial database if they put something on to the judicial database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that you would say we would like to see to get it copied already at that early stage and see whether that can be done. That's beyond at this moment my possibilities. I take it as a matter of fact that if that would have been possible that we would have used that facility as well. But please first discuss and see -- but let's first see if we can make the easy copy. If not, then please discuss the matter with the Registry whether there is a possibility to find a solution there. If not, we could come back to it and see whether the Chamber could further assist. But this is an area in which I feel the Chamber could not be of great help because these are operations which are beyond not only our control but even beyond our knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well sometimes I must say, Your Honour, occasionally some of the operations are beyond comprehension. But in this particular instance -- I mean, that may be a limit on my own comprehension but, Your Honour, the -- can I -- something that is, we suggest, within the remit of the Trial Chamber by way of authority. One must perhaps bear in mind the judicial database and what we are talking about now really are slightly different things. The judicial database has a wider purpose and enables people on one case to have material on another case. The really compelling priority for this case, Your Honour, is that the Trial Chamber in this case and the parties in this case should have this material as quickly as possible to deal with this case over the remaining period. Your Honour, one illustration of the point or one aspect of that is that we have been told, for example, that we would not be given exhibits which are -- where their admission is pending. Your Honour, from the point of view of this case, that really isn't very practical. Given apart from anything else the very rare instances where an exhibit which is pending is not ultimately exhibited, there would seem no practical reason for that limitation, that everything would be helpful to the parties and indeed to the Trial Chamber to have at this point. So would Your Honour -- well, first of all would Your Honour agree with that. If Your Honour's indicated that, then no doubt because there shouldn't be a technical problem. No doubt that would assist or encourage the Registry to say, well, yes, that limitation can go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter. I have to note, however, at this moment that one of the important reasons for not admitting exhibits very often, exhibits still pending, is that they are not translated which, of course, could cause some problem as well. Sometimes you have the B/C/S, sometimes you have the English, but we'll consider the matter and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's not a problem for us, Your Honour. That's the thing. It's a reason why -- of course, they shouldn't appear on the JDB until everything has been sorted out and they have been admitted but after all, this stuff normally comes from the parties in the first place. So for us to actually have it in usable form, in the same usable form, or the most usable form that anybody else has got it, which is really all we are asking and we are only asking for stuff to be copied over to us. If somebody in this building has material in a usable, accessible form, there doesn't seem to be any earthly reason why it simply shouldn't be copied over on to whatever medium, whether it's DVD or external hard drive, we request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know whether they are already scanned once they have not yet been admitted. That might be the reason. But as I said, we will consider the matter and we'll see whether we can accommodate the parties to the best of our abilities. Anything else, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, only that Mr. Haider, who has been very helpful, knows that we particularly if it's at all possible to put this stuff on, if it's going to be a DVD, it seems that may be adequate for this material, to have it today would be of tremendous assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, I worked on the matter yesterday late, 8.00, 9.00, with Mr. Zahar and Mr. -- it's really -- you should appreciate that I immediately and intensively pay attention to it and to try to resolve the matter as soon as possible. Don't push me any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour I'm not inviting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no I think, you, Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was going to express appreciation for Your Honour's work on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we have made our contribution. But I'm not asking Your Honours to do the DVD copying. I'm just asking for a DVD. It's five minutes, generally. I'm certainly not asking Your Honour to do that. That would be insolent of me and I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, may I say something? You said that I had sent a CD. You told me to get a draft of the constitution yesterday. I provided it on paper but also on CD, so that it can be given to my Defence team and they could make copies for both you and the Office of the Prosecutor because I have only one copy, one hard copy, so you have that both on paper and on CD, including the two maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- and it goes through the -- and whatever comes out of the detention unit has to fulfil all the formal requirements but I don't think it will take much time. Mr. Registrar informed me that he received it and it will be processed as usual. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just inquire of Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The CD with maps on that Your Honour referred to a few minutes ago, I don't know whether Mr. Krajisnik can answer this but Mr. Krajisnik gave me some time ago a CD with a number of maps on. Do you understand, Mr. Krajisnik, we are talking about the same material?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are probably talking about the same material. That's yesterday's map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a map of Sarajevo, and some maps taken from the book of Mr. -- Lord Owen, the Balkan Odyssey and, of course, a draft of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was adopted as a draft on the 28th of February. It turned out yesterday that that document was necessary. I wanted you to have that CD in order to have the draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure we will sort all this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll receive it within one or more hours and you will be able to look at what the content is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's very helpful, Your Honour. That's greatly appreciated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to turn to -- because it relates to the Cutileiro stuff that we were talking about yesterday, I'm going to turn to the 8th assembly session of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was held on the 25th of February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is P65, tab 93. That's the document. And I've got in the usual way a B/C/S copy for Mr. Krajisnik and I believe the interpreter's booth have it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I just swap over -- Mr. Krajisnik, may I just swap the copy I've given to you with another copy because it's got an additional note which is for my reference, thank you. These are the copies. Oh, I think I know what Mr. Tieger is going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a reminder about the ERNs, if you could repeat those, I can check those against the copy we had, as we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought Mr. Tieger had the information but I'm not complaining. It's SAO 25432. That's the B/C/S. And the English is -- well, it's the same, isn't it? 5434. It's a translation, 5434 to 5528. Is that -- that's what you're -- Mr. Tieger is after, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. That was the information. That's certainly the correct -- the same B/C/S that I understand is in evidence. I may have a different English translation, however. So I understand that the English translation in evidence is 00840431 through 0506.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's the same situation as yesterday. It's not the same one that I'm working from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be alert on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am alert to it but it was simply too late to redo that work, to make that adjustment. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you go, please, it's point number -- it's over on page 4 of the English. It's page 5 of the English, I beg your pardon, and it's page 3 of your version. There is briefing on Lisbon talks held on 21st and 22nd February 1992, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This meeting was taking place, wasn't it, Mr. Krajisnik, essentially between the two documents that we looked at yesterday, the two different stages of Cutileiro agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if this is the 25th of February, then it should be prior to that first document that was adopted before the 18th of March. This is a discussion that was endorsed in Lisbon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I was just trying to place it. There were -- it says here in the --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is related to the other two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But the Lisbon talks which are referred to here on the 21st and 22nd of February, those talks had produced the first of those documents we looked at yesterday, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the second of those documents, of course, lay in the future at this point, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm just saying that I don't know whether this first enactment was adopted at the first meeting in list been or at some other meeting in Lisbon because there were several. But it was certainly in Lisbon that the first document was adopted, the one that we discussed yesterday. That was produced by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps to avoid confusion, Mr. Krajisnik, we have seen two versions of this document but it was a -- it was a running discussion, wasn't it, in which there were several different versions of the document from time to time, more than just the two that we've seen in court?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm talking about the two versions that you presented here yesterday. The first version that highlights the years as a criterion is based on the negotiations that were held in Lisbon. So you're right on that. The second version is based on the negotiations that were held later, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour the reason I mentioned it is just for example at the foot of page 7 of the English version, Mr. Karadzic, I think it is, refers to second document, and I didn't want it to be supposed that it's as simple as a reference to the second document there being the second document that we are looking at because it is fairly clear this it wasn't and Mr. Krajisnik is confirming that, Your Honours. The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right, you are quite right, there were several versions and -- well, any way, this has to do with, how should I put this -- the first stage and it relies on the first document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: None of these three judges would ever expect a March document to be discussed in February. So it's -- and we have all the experience that if you prepare a document, that it usually has different versions so that's all obvious. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At page 10 of the English, Mr. Krajisnik, and it's also page 10 of the Serbian, do you see a point 2 in the margin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And this is still Mr. Karadzic speaking. He says, "Next -- in their first document, they proposed the 1981 census, the Croats however apparently asked that it be based on the 1971 census while the Muslims suggested the one from 1991, so it probably will be 1981 after all. Next, it was noted in the existing municipalities as well, with minor adjustments which would be clearly documented, (for instance contiguous villages in a Serbian or a Muslim municipality would be joined together and vice versa which is what we are already doing in such a way that municipalities would be ground in a corresponding constituent unit in one -- in which one particular nation had a clear majority." [as read] Mr. Krajisnik, when Mr. Karadzic was saying which is what we are already doing, was in fact the -- a process of contiguous villages being joined together already underway?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the plebiscite was carried out, certain peripheral settlements, Serb settlements, also expressed their views at local level, stating that they should be part of a municipality where Serbs are a majority. So that would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, my question was really whether that was happening anywhere in a practical sense, as opposed to a declaration of intention.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not practically carried through but - how should I put this? - people expressed their will as to what constituent unit they would like to belong to. So what was envisaged here was something that people locally expressed by way of their own will. It wasn't that it was verified as something final. It was an ongoing process.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then if we carry on the next paragraph, Mr. Karadzic says, "A constituent unit may consist of a number of separate parts. There means that the republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina may not have continuous territory. It may have several separate territories and although the map we have drawn up would connect all the parts, the whole of the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, it would leave the Muslims in five to six enclaves, Croats in two to three." Mr. Krajisnik, did that reflect what you alluded to yesterday afternoon, which was that each -- each of the parties to these discussions was producing its own maps, its own proposals which were in favour, in its own favour?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it wasn't -- it wasn't so much -- this is right, there wasn't an insistence by the Serbs at that time on continuous territory but that was your negotiating position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. But that came later. The territorial element was introduced too, namely that the parties could agree on an exchange of territories in order to establish continuity, especially for units to consist of several parts. That's something that the Croat side insisted on. They had Posavina and they had a majority in western Herzegovina so it was impossible for those regions to be linked up. But we were certainly ready at that point to find a solution by way of compromise, by peaceful means, although it did not suit us. We would have wanted to have territories that were linked up, but we still agreed to what you read out just now, that this constituent Serb unit did not have to consist of a single whole. That was the first stage of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go on to page 14 of the English and it's page 15 in the Serbian, we find -- and it's Professor Koljevic talking now, we find a paragraph beginning, "Of the major issues." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Koljevic, of course, was part of the negotiating team. "Of the major issues we failed to ensure the connection with the other segments of the Serbian people and as we repeatedly said of the Croatian people with Croatia as well, because quite naturally, in this, we have a common interest. However, there are indications that that might be possible too." Do you recall, Mr. Krajisnik, is that correct, that there had been indications that it might be possible for you to connect up the different Serb areas?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a major issue. Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina naturally wanted to live together with Croats from Croatia. Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to be in Yugoslavia so that they would be with the rest of the Serb people. So what he's saying here is that we did not get what we wanted for Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain in Yugoslavia. So implicitly he's saying that we made a compromise so this is a major issue. Implicitly we gave up on Yugoslavia but we got these other things, as Mr. Koljevic says. So my interpretation is that that is it as far as this major issue is concerned. As for Bosnia-Herzegovina, I can give an answer to your question if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, yes, my next question -- well, it says, yes, I am interested.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a series of documents, I'm now talking only about the Serbian side and about the position of the Serbian side. When some sort of preliminary map was drafted, was drawn, we realised that there was not enough connection between Serbian territories, and since the territorial principle applied, we have documents from the time when we had bilateral talks with the Croatian side about certain concessions to be made to them in central Bosnia, in the area of Kupres and concessions to be made to us that would have the purpose of linking our two major enclaves. That was in our interest. Other parties as well expressed their interests. I'll just give you an example. In order to satisfy certain interests, we looked at solutions from Israel, whereby some people would have a passage from their territory into another territory that belonged to them, passing through --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, one of the members of my team is suggesting that you are probably going too fast for interpretation or -- and others. You probably -- it's in your own interest, probably, Mr. Krajisnik, to take it a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always criticise people who spoke fast. I thought -- well, I'll try. I kindly ask you to caution me about this because I really want to speak properly. Thank you for telling me. If you wish, I can repeat something, if there has been any omissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps just -- if you would just carry on from where you were.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically, I was saying that the problem of this linking of territories was less important if Bosnia was an internationally recognised state, and if a constituent unit can be linked up and we could have if we were to barter certain territories with the Croats or possibly with the Muslims, because these were small problems. Then that is what we advocated. However, it wasn't even a problem if a Croat or a Muslim territory was separated, like western Bosnia, Cazinska Krajina, which is impossible to be linked up. There would be freedom of movement, it would be one state, so there is no reason for that not to be implemented, if possible. If it is possible to have a link-up, then it would be desirable because it would be better to have a single whole, if I can put it that way. So we insisted that this be carried out within Bosnia-Herzegovina, that our constituent unit would later be linked up. Here we said that it could consist of several parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How -- when Mr. Koljevic was saying there are indications that might be possible, how strong had such indications been?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, well, there was something that was there all the time, that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be a link between Serbia and Croatia and that there shouldn't be any borders there or passports. I presented an example here, that Mr. Izetbegovic at the end of 1991 saying at the congress of the SDA there should be no passports or borders on the Drina or the Una. Croats should not feel that they are imprisoned in Bosnia or that Serbs had passports on the Drina River. So this process of bringing people of the same nation together was later resolved by having every constituent unit given the right to establish special ties with neighbouring states, and neighbouring states are Serbia, or rather Yugoslavia, and Croatia. That's what Mr. Koljevic said. It is important for us to have spiritual links, cultural links, and the situation right now is the way it is. That is to say we stay in Bosnia. I know, since he is from that field himself, that is his own line of work, he always advocated these cultural ties, and also that these cultural links can be a way of replacing state links, in terms of Yugoslavia. He's talking about Croatia here. That's why I said this. He's talking about Croats with Croatia. That is why I included this in this particular line of thought that was present at the time. This was ultimately verified in Dayton and there were these special relations, special ties, that existed in every agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, a couple of paragraphs -- well, no, a bit further actually. A page or so further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's page 16 of the English, Your Honour, Dr. Karadzic begins to speak again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you just find that as a reference point, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's actually a bit further on probably but a page or so further on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then I'm going to go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is actually on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I didn't notice, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Something very minor. First of all, with the exception of pagination difference, probably arising from some format issue at the beginning of the document, it appears to be precisely the same document, both the English translations, word for word, but the pagination issue means that I would ask Mr. Stewart to give us a little time to find the corresponding reference in the copy we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's good news and a perfectly fair request, Your Honour, so I'll do exactly that. So we got Dr. Karadzic and then I want to go two or three pages on, skipping over Dr. Karadzic's announcement that Scotland had announced its secession which is news that hadn't actually got as far as England at that point. On page 19 of the English, it's in -- right in the middle of page 19, a paragraph, "if BH is to be independent then we have to make sure there are three independent BHs." It's probably around -- around page 20 in Serbian, that passage. There are references to -- there are references to Broz, and we know about him [indiscernible] and so on, there is a paragraph referring to 1971, 1974, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Broz, 71, yes, I found it. It's on page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. It's immediately preceding paragraph -- that very short paragraph, "If BH is to be independent, then we have to make sure that there are three independent BHs," Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Krajisnik we see all sorts of fluid terms perhaps in the course of some of these discussions. When Dr. Karadzic is saying there are we have to make sure there are three independent Bosnia and Herzegovinas, what did you understand him to mean there by three independent Bosnia and Herzegovinas. Independent in what way to what degree?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly what Mr. Karadzic meant when he said this. This is a speech made by a man who attended negotiations, who was in a way trying to justify this new concept of ours. Now we keep talking about an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina whereas we put Yugoslavia into the constitution. That is why very often he inserts illogical things that are receptive to the ears of that group which, all the time, like Mrs. Plavsic last time when we were discussing this, keep saying, what kind of solution is this? We are not in Yugoslavia. At this moment, when we were discussing this, Mr. Karadzic knew quite clearly and we had accepted that, that there would be only one internationally recognised entity and that is Bosnia-Herzegovina. You saw that he's not saying "state" but "internationally recognised entity." One chair in the UN. But when he's saying this, before parliament, then he is introducing quite a few political elements, quite simply in order to blunt the opportunism of those who disagree with that, those who want Yugoslavia or something else. I saw here that you in the West look at each and every word quite literally, whereas this is politics. He didn't mean that. He knew that we had accepted Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is no denying that, but then the MPs are listening to him so that's different. He's offering sort of a carrot, something that people like to hear. You will see that in the constitution that was adopted and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then if we go on about a page and a bit, it's page 19 of the English, it's probably going to be page 20 of the -- or even 21 of the Serbian. It will be on page 20 or 21, still in Mr. Karadzic's speech, he says, "Take this thing in Krajina yesterday. I can bet you that Alija will pay off every Krajina deputy in pure gold." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it's page -- I think it's page 21, almost the last full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you are always so helpful. Thank you. Yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm sorry I was just giving Their Honours an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, I'm sorry, but you're talking about page 19 for that last paragraph? And we are on page 17 in our version. In our draft, it's page 17. So it's a bit disturbing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- if that's -- yes, I see. Mr. Tieger was asking for the opportunity to be able to find that different reference. I can at the moment -- I'm afraid, Your Honour, I can only give the page reference in the document that I've got. It might be that when Mr. Tieger has -- if I could invite his services, if Mr. Tieger has then found the reference on his, he could give it quickly to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would be pleased to do that. I was just going to suggest that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's excellent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the most recent reference is found at the bottom of page 18 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He says, "Take this thing in Krajina yesterday. I can bet you that Alija will pay off every Krajina deputy in pure gold for what they weigh just so that we leave Sarajevo and we abandon the idea that Sarajevo will be the capital of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina. Banja Luka will, of course, be the capital of Bosnian Krajina. The Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina will have counties and regions because it is easier to share power that way. They will also be responsible for development and so forth. But leaving Sarajevo where there are 215.000 Serbs, including Yugoslavs, where there are great riches, if we left Sarajevo, well, we should be hanged." Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, as appears clearly from that paragraph, well, we see it also clearly later in this document, is it fair to say there was at the very least there was intense irritation among the leadership, including Mr. Karadzic and you, at the proposal coming from the Krajina that Banja Luka might become the capital of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, irritating is perhaps not an appropriate word but I can explain what this is all about. I was saying something earlier on too so in case you're interested. Well, at any rate we didn't agree. I didn't agree. The majority didn't agree with what had been done in Krajina at that moment and Mr. Karadzic said that. I can explain what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik I am inviting you to do exactly that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem of rivalry between Banja Luka and Sarajevo originates from the system that existed before the multi-party elections. Sarajevo was favoured. There were six centres, one of them was Bihac, then Banja Luka, Zenica, Tuzla, Mostar, and Sarajevo. I don't know if I missed any. So Banja Luka as a centre fell in terms of economic development on to the 22nd place. People from there, qualified staff, were taken to Sarajevo to make their contribution to the development of Sarajevo. When we remained alone, and when I say alone I mean in the assembly, that animosity also carried with it certain tensions. Therefore, the deputies from Krajina, in the framework of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, put forward a demand saying the time has come to build the constituent unit of the Serbian people. Let the capital of that constituent unit be Banja Luka. And the contribution to the discussion of Mr. Karadzic and many other people was that it wouldn't be fair for us not to have a part of Sarajevo because there were a lot of Serbs in Sarajevo and we often made comparisons with Jerusalem where two ethnic communities are intertwined and keep saying that they have a claim on a part of Jerusalem, both the Jews and the Palestinians. So the same demand was made later, on the 25th or 26th of July, at the session of the Assembly of the Serbian People during the war. People of Krajina loved their town and they wanted Banja Luka for once to be a capital. I'll remind you that Banja Luka in the times of the kingdom of Yugoslavia was a centre of so-called Banovina, and in socialist times its rating fell to the 22nd place. And Vogosca was twice less developed than Banja Luka. So this regionalisation, they thought, should not only be designed on the basis of political criteria but also on the basis of economic criteria. They said -- so they favoured Banja Luka whereas we were saying that it was not a good idea to leave Banja Luka -- to leave Sarajevo, because we had a stake there and a lot of Serb population there. It's not that we were against Banja Luka itself. That's what Mr. Karadzic was trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that the only difference or issue there was between you and the Serb leadership in the Krajina at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the only difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what was the other difference or what were the other differences?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The greatest part of the Serb population in the then Bosnian Krajina, that is the part of Krajina that is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were 60 or maybe 65 per cent of Serbs on that side, or maybe the division was 55 versus 45 per cent, and it was quite natural, and I talked about that historic moment before, that there were many attempts to create that region as a sociopolitical community, to turn it into something autonomous, a republic of sorts or something. Detached from the rest of the Serb population in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was not a good thing for Serbs, and it could have been interpreted as a tear-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Maybe apart from advocating Banja Luka as a capital, there was another element to this, advocating an idea that Banja Luka should be a separate constituent unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's the second problem. And a third problem was that those two Krajinas historically always strove to unite because for a long time they belonged to two different states, including in the Vance plan, but the Krajina people thought that they were separated and wanted to unite. And their internal coherence was much stronger than the ties in the rest of the population. However, by that time, we had already accepted the Vance plan and if we had given in to the demands of the people from Krajina, we could have opened ourselves to accusations that we were trying to destroy something that we had already accepted, and it was a big problem to explain to them why we couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then if we look at point 5, it's the middle of page 20 of my English version, and it's page 22 in your version, Mr. Krajisnik. It's almost halfway down page 22.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've found number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Karadzic says, "Our strategic goals are beginning to materialise. The opposition in Serbia is not right. Our people here in BH are also not right." Are you able to say what were at that point the strategic goals as they were beginning to materialise?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely an example of what I was saying a moment ago. Mr. Karadzic keeps changing his rhetoric all the time, at least very often. He is now replying to the opposition from Serbia who were saying that somebody's betraying the Serb people, closing them in within Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of course, this was a very uninformed opinion. And he is saying, our strategic goal is to have authority over our own unit, avoiding outvoting or minority status, and in order to make it more palatable to his audience he's saying that if these internal borders are thicker than the outside borders, so what? We'll strive for the internal borders to be suitable. When you are pushing a project which is meeting with a lot of resistance, a lot of differing desires and ambitions, this sort of rhetoric is understandable. He keeps trying to explain that we had to look for a solution within Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then he's spicing it up with remarks like, we'll strife to make it thicker or thinner, et cetera. He already knows that we won't be part of Yugoslavia but he dares not -- he dare not say it because the people are not yet ready to accept it. It's not that we were doing one thing and saying another. We were trying to be realistic as politicians and to defend and promote Serb interests to the greatest possible extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then two or three paragraphs below that, it's the foot of page 20, very foot of page 20 on my English, and it will -- you see you start to speak, Mr. Krajisnik. It's the top of page 23 in your copy. Do you see that? "I thank you, Dr. Karadzic and Professor Koljevic. Mr. Karadzic was right when he said we would all answer to the people for our actions, that is why everyone has to judge his own actions to make sure that we act for the benefit of the people we represent. I thank him particularly for what he did not say, what he was going to address to the people -- for what he did not say. What he was going to address to the people of Krajina. Because if he had said what he was going to this morning, then the people of Krajina would probably know what he meant, because what the people of Krajina had done was assessed as bad, I have to say this in his name and Mr. Koljevic's, and it was not wise at this point. That's why our decision at today's session of the assembly must be wise and I propose that you have heard as introductory remarks be the main item -- that what you have heard as introductory remarks be the main item from the agenda. Let us have a discussion on the constitution and the laws, to get over with the Thursday meeting which we intend to hold with the mediation of the UN, then we will adopt the constitution and the laws." There is a meeting coming up, isn't there, with the EC people, in particular, Mr. Cutileiro. That's what that means, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you point out 66 deputies are present. Then you say, "As I was a participant in the Lisbon talks, I would like to add a few remarks. Today we must discuss the first item which is crucial for the Serbian people. Gentlemen, we have two options. One to fight by political means, to make the most out of the present time, as a first phase, or to break off the talks and go for what we have done over the centuries, win our own territories by force." Now in putting forth those two possibilities, Mr. Krajisnik, were there -- or was there among those 66 deputies any significant faction that was leaning towards the second of those options, to break off the talks and win our own territories by force?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody was in favour of war, and if you allow me I want to explain what I meant by this. As a participant in the negotiations since I chaired the sessions, I rarely took the floor to add to what Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic had to say about those negotiations and their course. But whenever I felt that we were running out of arguments for something that would be reasonable to accept, then I did take the floor. I said a bit further up that I was supporting Karadzic and I said it was a good thing he didn't tell the Krajina people about Banja Luka, what he had intended to say to them. By saying that, I wanted to pressure people to tell them that they should be more reasonable in their thinking, and I told them that we had to choose between two options, either to negotiate or to fight, fighting implying suffering. So I was warning them, in fact, if we don't want to negotiate, then we have to fight, and the war is something that is very bad for us. I -- Pasic and a lot of our history so if you read this in Serbian it's clear, we had two options, one being to negotiate and if we don't want to negotiate we are left with the second option, that needs no explanation. It's self explanatory. So if you put it to people like that, I was saying that we cannot negotiate amongst ourselves. I cannot say that this introductory discussion was accepted. Nobody was against negotiations. Maybe some people said something in jest, but they also didn't realise how difficult it was to negotiate. They thought, "Ha, it's going to be easy to achieve what we want." They didn't realise that we can only achieve something that is realistic to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go on, Mr. Krajisnik, then, the next speaker is Mrs. Plavsic, and then after that Professor Ajdanovic speaks and he starts at the top of page 26 of what you've got and towards the top of page 23 of my English version. Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it's Professor Najdanovic, the initial N is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's missing in the original, so that's helpful to jot that in, Professor Najdanovic. I'm not sure if we come across him before, Mr. Krajisnik. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Najdanovic was a deputy, an MP. He was also on the political council. He's an ethnic Serb and he worked as professor in the medical school of the university and unfortunately he had stayed behind in Sarajevo because his wife was about to give birth, and the gangs that roamed around Sarajevo at the time slaughtered him. He was a wonderful, very reasonable man. Excuse me, Mr. Stewart, I reviewed what I said yesterday, and I made a slip of the tongue yesterday, saying that the head of our delegation in bilateral negotiations was Mr. Koljevic. But it was in fact Mr. Karadzic. I just remembered it this moment. It wasn't Mr. Koljevic who headed our delegation in our talks with the Muslims and the Croats but Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well it's helpful, Mr. Krajisnik, always, to have that tidied up. Thank you. So where Professor Najdanovic is speaking there a third paragraph, he says, "I would like to say that the Lisbon agreement was a great successes of our representatives. There agreement remains to be fine tuned and this will be our chance for modifications to improve our positions. I would not tie our present position on these negotiations to our strategic goal. We must not find ourselves in a dilemma similar to the Babic-Milosevic situation. We all knew that many of Babic's objections were justified and yet we did not support him but Milosevic. Why? Because at the time only certain things are feasible. Europe and America are insisting that the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina must not be changed. Failing to understand that would be political -- unpolitical and unwise. However, getting Europe to agree to our sovereignty, even if only within the BH borders is important enough and it's up to us what we will do with the sovereignty." So he is referring there to the underlying -- well, no, I'll put it entirely neutrally. What is he referring to there as our strategic goal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, late Mr. Najdanovic explained it. The strategic goal, namely that the Serb people have sovereignty over themselves without being outvoted and in the position of a minority ruled by somebody else, was the basis. So if we get a constituent unit with some sort of limited sovereignty, because there are joint institutions envisaged, he says that that's fine because it's within a reasonable framework, considering that Europe and the United States are advocating unchangeable borders, and that's an example of our work in Lisbon and our negotiations. So you have certain target units within which you can move. Our strategic goal was equality with the other ethnic communities and power to rule our people, meaning that we didn't want to be outvoted. We didn't want our lands to be neglected. I am -- I don't know what the other two sides were thinking, what their rationale was, but I'm explaining the rationale of the Serb side. So this round of negotiations in Lisbon was a great success, and that's what he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then he continues, about two -- well, it's just two paragraphs further on. He says, "In further negotiations ..." Top of page 24 of my English version and it's the top of page 27 in -- on your don't, Mr. Krajisnik. "In further negotiations, whether the issue is dual citizenship or multiple passports, we must not go below a certain minimum. That minimum is uninterrupted ties, spiritual, economic, geographic with the other Serbian lands, above all with our mother country. It is my personal belief that this federal BiH will not be able to avoid the destiny of the federal Yugoslavia. Let us ensure that it is federal to the same degree that Yugoslavia was federal after 1974. To me this is a provisional stage, a transitional state, pending the final parting of ways." He's -- Mr. Krajisnik, do you understand him to be saying there, "let's do this because my prediction is that Bosnia will break up anyway in future in the same way that Yugoslavia is breaking up now"? Is that a summary of what he's saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that -- look at what he said just before that. This reference was made so that the previous thing would be more palatable. But that was not the point. The point was that a success was achieved in Lisbon and we should accept that and we shouldn't be afraid of the future Bosnia-Herzegovina because we would have our own sovereignty and that's a great success.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then it's at the foot of the English, page 24, the English version that I have, and then it's fairly near the top of page 28 in your version, Mr. Krajisnik. He says, "First" -- it's a very short paragraph, it's a single line, something or other, says, "First the issue of Serbian access to the sea." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, without going into it at this point but we know that the Serbian access to the sea emerged as number 6 of the strategic goals that were published eventually in the Official Gazette and were discussed later on, on the 12th of May at the Banja Luka assembly session. At this point, in February 1992, was the issue of Serbian access to the sea a matter that had been under discussion among the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is yes, but not only within the Serbian leadership. We talked to the Croatian side. I don't know whether it was at this stage, but we talked also to late President Tudjman, and it was clearly stated, he said it, it was not natural for Serbs to be able to see the sea and not have any access to it. And an agreement was made in Dayton, I can give you that example, it was signed, although it wasn't signed in Paris, where a triple barter of territories was supposed to be made so that we would have access to the sea in Prevlaka peninsula. But the second option was that Bosnia did have access to the sea at Neum, and we were saying that if Bosnia had access to the sea, then it was natural that each constituent unit should have part of that access. How? That was another matter. Let me just add this. Croatia, the Croatian state, was interested, had a stake in a narrow belt just above Dubrovnik, and if we had access to the sea at Prevlaka then that would solve the problems of Serbia and Montenegro and Yugoslavia as well. That principle that we should have access to the sea as a constituent unit was never in dispute, although it required negotiations with Croatia and with the other two sides. And all that is documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand there is some excellent and helpful communication going on from Mr. Haider up into cyberspace and back down to Mr. Mujanovic. We do appreciate that very much. Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock. Would that be a convenient point for Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would give me one second with Mr. Haider. Mr. Krajisnik, you asked whether we could provide you with a DVD of the early part of the 25th of April session. It has been prepared and Mr. Haider will hand it out to you now so that it's available to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I already commended Mr. Haider for being the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll not tell Ms. Philpott. We will adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we were looking at Professor Najdanovic's contribution and he's talking about access to the sea, and after that reference, he makes a reference to TV programmes. Do you see, I'm not going to read this paragraph, it's just for the reference point. Do you see a paragraph beginning, "So far from TV programmes"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the last sentence of that same paragraph, he says, "Our goal has to be access to the sea where Serbs come closest to it, which is Serbian Herzegovina." And then it has brackets, a deputy, "We have already done that, Professor." Applauded by several deputies. What did that mean, Mr. Krajisnik? Was it just some humorous intervention? In what sense had it already been done?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this deputy meant. Unless he was alluding to the war that was being waged around Dubrovnik. However, this is not serious. It is wrong to make jokes of that kind, and has nothing to do with our standpoint. I assume that that was it because otherwise there is no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: After that intervention by a deputy, Professor Najdanovic continues, "What we must do as of today is to communicate to the Serbian people that it must be prepared for territorial changes, for relocation of populations, the familiar tune of betrayal of the Serbian people is easily invoked these days. Regardless of pain, the global goals of the nation must take priority. We must be ready to give some krags [phoen] in Krajina for other krags, only this time from Metkovic to Dubrovnik and this means gaining access to the sea." First, Mr. Krajisnik, did you understand Professor Najdanovic's reference to being prepared for territorial changes, for relocation of populations, to relate to matters wider than the matter of access to the sea?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is his personal point of view. First of all, let me talk about access to the sea. This is a megalomaniac claim, that we should give a strip of land alongside the border between Croatia and western Bosnia, that is to say Cazinska Krajina with Livna [phoen]. That's why he was referring to these krags, in order to have more access to the sea. That was not realistic. But he said that, well, as a manner of speaking. As for relocating the population, perhaps he thought that if we were changing some parts with Croatia, that then people from Croatia with which Serbs were at war, if I can put it that way, well, would lead to a relocation of population in that part of territory that would be exchanged. So this is exchanging Bosnia-Herzegovinian territories which would belong to the Serb constituent unit with the Croatian state that had already been recognised. That's what he meant, that there would be these relocations because by then Serbs were already fleeing from the Croat part to the Serb areas. So as far as I can tell, that is what Mr. Najdanovic had in mind here because access to the sea is being referred to as the central issue, and that is what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- in relation either to access to the sea or broader issues of changes to the map, I'll put it that way, changes to the map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did the Bosnian Serb leadership at this time discuss the need to communicate to the Serbian people that there might be a need for relocation of populations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said what Mr. Karadzic was saying in case there were a war, but possibly somebody gave a free interpretation along those lines. But what is referred to here is a political solution, where it didn't cross anybody's mind to have any kind of intentional relocations of the population. I have to highlight something. The late president of Croatia, Tudjman, was being quoted as saying that there should be humane relocations of the population. I don't know whether he said that or not but it was ascribed to him at any rate. So perhaps that would be that idea, freely interpreted, but I'm saying that the policy of the Serb side in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the political negotiations carried out, did not advocate relocations of the population at all. What was advocated was the establishment of constituent units where somebody would be a minority, somebody would be a majority. Where we were in the majority that would be a Serbian unit and we would govern ourselves, and, of course, the others would be there in the other territory. Now, whether somebody would do something through his own free will is a different matter. I am confident that there are no official statements to that effect. Well, perhaps at a regional level somebody said something but our policy in negotiations and in agreements as you will see was invariably that even if somebody left after the war had broken out, that they had to go back to their homes. This was at the very beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then if we go on, Mr. Krajisnik, it's page 28 of my English version, and it's at page 32 of your version of this document, we have got towards the end of a reasonably long contribution by a Mr. Vojnovic, and Mr. Vojnovic was who? He was presumably a deputy. Where was he from? I beg your pardon. I'm so sorry, it isn't Mr. Vojnovic, it's Mr. Miskin. We have come across him. It's against the number 8 in your margin. There is a paragraph beginning, "Briefly on borders," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Briefly on borders, regional borders must be drawn up on the basis of the decision of citizens of each village, municipality and region as to where they want to live, although this is a complex job it can be done quite successfully." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, I would -- you -- you would agree it was a complex job?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A complex job, because throughout the negotiations, it was only the borders or rather the maps that were a problem that could not be solved. All the rest was easy to solve. Well, easy; easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I would like you to look at some maps now, please. Could you be given -- it was D7B, I think it was. That was the map which you said was attached to Cutileiro agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if in the first place we could have P211. Perhaps we could have P211 up on the ELMO or however we get it on to the screen. I'm not sure how practical that is. Perhaps we should do it the other way around, then. It's simply too big, I think, to be -- thank you. Yes. I remember we had it yesterday so there must be some way of doing it. My thanks to the Prosecution for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want you to have another map as well, Mr. Krajisnik. We are going to have to look at three maps, as best we can, alongside each other, and this one is the one that we glanced at yesterday, really, P293, which was in P68, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm entirely in Your Honours' hands as to whether at some point Your Honours would have it more convenient to have a different map up on the ELMO and precisely how we look at them but we have got three maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to you what should be on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes well, I'll do it in the first place, Your Honour, but I'm certainly inviting Your Honours to make any request that would help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you have a shopping bag with a file. Was that -- you were just checking something, were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get anything out. I just wanted to see a similar map but please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Krajisnik. We can see you didn't in the end get anything out. Right. Mr. Krajisnik, you've got this map, P293, have you, in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Now, first of all, what do you understand this map to be?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is this the map that you're referring to, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I just double check that it is? I feel sure it is but I just want to be 100 per cent sure. Yes, it is, indeed. Yes, first of all, what do you understand that map to be?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an ethnic map, similar to the other map but it was just subdivided into even smaller parts. One municipality here is divided into settlements. You see this map, the one that you can see now, that was the basis for Cutileiro's map, especially -- I beg your pardon. Here, where Prijedor is, if you look at that part, and if you compare it to the map that you saw a few moments ago, everything is half green because the municipality is 51 per cent, whereas here, if you look at the local communes and the villages, then you see that the micro-division is different from that of the entire municipality. This was a basis for our map, the Serb map, and for Cutileiro's map and all other maps that were presented as a proposal to the European Community for them in turn to give their proposal. That's why I said that throughout all negotiations this map was the subject of the debate that took place - not Mr. Okun's map, if I can call it that - because what Mr. Miskin was saying could not be applied in that case. You can see here that there are certain imaginary lines that were later drawn into the maps of the entities. Cutileiro's map. So please whether we discuss this in the future it would be a good thing for you to compare both maps. You can compare this map to the Cutileiro map. You will see how similar it is because it was this micro-plan. And the imaginary line which was later drawn between the entities, it said here that these small villages could opt for one entity or the other. So that was the basis when the maps were actually being drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One point, I just want to clarify with you, Mr. Krajisnik, this the map P293, it's the -- the more complicated map, its ethnic structure of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina according to the first results of 1991 census, and although it's very tiny letters and probably younger eyes than mine could confirm, in the very bottom right-hand corner of this document, it says, "Publisher, faculty of geography, Belgrade," and as best I can do, 1992. If we can have general agreement it says 1992, I would feel reassured. That's what younger eyes say as well, Mr. Krajisnik. The -- we were here in February March 1992. Do you actually know whether this particular map was available to you at the time of these Cutileiro talks in February and March 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm surprised that this is 1992 because we had it from the very outset. We had this map from the very outset from the beginning of the negotiations. So it should date back to at least January 1992. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop everyone there. Publishing in 1992 doesn't mean that it did not exist before. I would say publishing is totally different from --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was going to put that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a detail. Mr. Krajisnik said it was the basis on which he works. Of course I do not know -- is this to be contested, Mr. Harmon? No? Then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm certainly happy to proceed on the basis one would suppose that the people involved probably had some priority over the general public in obtaining such material.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So Mr. Krajisnik, you had this map. The -- for example, let's take an example. That large swathe of what I'll call Croat territory in the southwest of Bosnia, you -- we can all see and understand what I mean, and you understand what I mean, Mr. Krajisnik, do you, if I use that -- that term and you're pointing to it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Exactly that. Towards the north and in the centre is a small piece, relatively small, of course, a relatively small piece of land or territory which is marked as a -- Serb absolute ethnic majority. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're probably referring to this, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Actually, no, I'm not. I'm going down south -- yes, you're nearly there. No, further down the page, to the south, a little bit further, Mr. Krajisnik, a couple of centimetres further. You're nearly there. It's just to the right of where you've got the pointer there. It's a smaller piece of territory than what you were pointing to a moment ago. Do you see that? It's a little blob of --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in fact immediately above that is a very similar-sized piece of territory which is marked as Muslim absolute majority, isn't it? It's immediately to the north. It's a similar size and shape, really. Do you see?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It cannot be seen very well here but, yes, I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fact, there is a finely little piece of relatively -- relatively tiny little piece of Muslim-marked territory just to the southwest or west-southwest of that blue marked piece of territory. Do you also see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The colours cannot be seen properly here, but I assume that it's sort of left to this, right? On the screen you cannot really tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the colours are terribly difficult to see on the screen. You probably will need to glance over at the paper.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I think I [Previous interpretation continues]... if I may do that, Your Honour. I can give Mr. Krajisnik an additional copy of this map so that he's got it at his elbow because the colours are naturally more distinct on the paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we take the Serb area --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as the centre of the clock it would be approximately between 7 and 8.00, what you referred to; is that correct, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, yes, it would. Well, yes, 6 minutes past 8 or something, Your Honour is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So we got that, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, it can be seen much better here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it -- would it be correct to say as a starting point that -- but please say straight away if it isn't correct, Mr. Krajisnik, that in this complex job that might be faced of drawing up borders and so on, that this pieces of territory like this would be among the most difficult to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're right, but such small parts would actually stay within Croatian territory because they were not along the imaginary inter-entity ethnic line. We could not resolve it the same way we could in other places. We could not put the Muslim ones into the Muslim entity the Serb ones into the Serb entity, because they were within Croatian territory in depth. How should I put this? They are not very big. They would remain as a minority within the Croat entity. I think. I assume that that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If I put something to you, Mr. Krajisnik, again, as see whether you agree with this, that perhaps paradoxically I put it to you that the most difficult to deal with, your answer suggests that in a paradoxical way they were the easiest to deal with because it was really clear that no major adjustment was feasible in relation to pieces of territory like that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. That was the most difficult thing to solve. When I said it was the easiest, I meant it's simply impossible to solve. It remains unsolved or solved in an unfair way. It was a situation that was imposed on us. But you are right in saying that these little units were the most difficult to place within their mother entity. They would remain within another entity, and you can see from Cutileiro's map that they remained within the Croat entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the -- what was -- it was perhaps early days, Mr. Krajisnik, but within the Bosnian Serb leadership, at the time you were discussing these matters at the Cutileiro talks, what was your thinking about what would happen to, for example, the Serb population in that relatively small area of Serb majority land that we have just been considering?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you what happened but there is a statement of mine from that time. What I'm going to say now is also written somewhere. There would have been reciprocity. They would remain as a minority within that entity because it's not possible for every village, if you have three entities, it's not possible for every village, every local commune, to become part of their own entity, and you can find one of my statements made to the media to the effect that these Herzegovinas, eastern and western, would have reciprocity between them and there would be protection of the fundamental human rights for the Croats who remain in the eastern part of Herzegovina and we expect the same of them with regard to Serbs who remain within their entity. And when I say human rights, I mean in particular those very sensitive ethnic rights, and that was the primary consideration, even more important than economic and other considerations that are -- that normally come first in every day life. And when I say that this -- when this Cutileiro map was drawn, it went without saying, it was implied that most Muslims should be within the Muslim entity, most Croats within the Croat entity, et cetera but a certain number would remain within the entities of another ethnic community as a minority. That was implied. We were not looking to draw borders of new states. We were looking for an internal transformation. And you will find in Mr. Cutileiro's map that this belongs to the Croat entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was -- was it first of all among the Bosnian Serb negotiators in those talks, was it your expectation that if Cutileiro plan was agreed and did come to be implemented, that the population, the Serb population of a place such as that that we just identified, would stay where they were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry but I'll have to refer to another statement of mine that I made on the 12th of May where I put it in a crude way, saying that I know that my home place will remain within Muslimania but please let's have most Serbs the majority of Serbs within the Serb unit. All participants from the negotiations from the Serb side were aware that a certain number of Serbs will have to remain within other entities. And the same would be true of smaller numbers of Muslims and Croats. We have figures. In 1992, in what is Republika Srpska today, the Muslims were 23 per cent, 17 and 5 per cent were Croats. Whereas in today's federation, the percentage of Serbs was 36 per cent. Those are -- or those were the facts. You can't do anything with it. That's the way we were laid out, and that was not a problem. Today's figures from 2000, and I can give you the documents and the information prepared both in English and in Serbian by the authorities, of course, they would be a minority. We realised that. And I have to say, Mr. Stewart, when we talked at our assembly sessions, there were people who came from Zenica, let's say, or some other areas that had been within the Muslim entity for a long time, they said, "What's going to become much us? We made our decision at the plebiscite and we have to stay with them." And there were some inadequate remarks made, but the real crux of the matter is what I just said. It's impossible for everyone to end up within their own entity. Nor was it ever our objective, ours or Mr. Cutileiro's because it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But was your -- this -- these pieces of land we have been talking to, it seems pretty clear from the map that they were in Tomislavgrad. That can be relatively easily seen. The -- was it your expectation that either the whole or very near to the whole of the Serb residents in that Serb-majority piece of land we were looking at would in fact choose to stay living where they were after implementation if it should happen of Cutileiro plan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to add to this, to correct what Mr. Miskin said, Mr. Cutileiro's plan envisaged that people should their intentions as divided by that interethnic line. It was not envisaged that people would declare where they wanted to live in those places deep into the territory of an entity. That would have been unreasonable. But you will find it in the principles that where this inter-entity line was drawn, then such settlements would have to choose which side they would go to. And that would be an expression of their political will. It would have been illogical to apply the same to some areas that are deep into the territory of one entity.
