But to answer your question, as regards larger territories such as around Prijedor, we even thought about enclaves that would have a certain degree of autonomy, and that would be subject to negotiation because it's not the same thing as a small village. Those were larger enclaves that would have some cultural or other rights within that constituent unit. We tried to satisfy the largest number of people in each of the three ethnic communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We -- I remember this bit of the discussion where we discussed an enclave and it was envisaged in Cutileiro's plan that this enclave would be half Croat, half Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We will come that in a moment, Mr. Krajisnik. The question which arises out of what you've said is this: I'm not asking you now about what the Serb population, for example, of that piece of land in Tomislavgrad might have been asked to declare at any point. I'm asking what your expectation was, as to what the -- what the individual families and residents would actually do if this plan was implemented broadly, as seen on this map and under discussion. What did you expect they would actually do, the people that lived there? Would they stay? Would they go?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We expected that everybody would remain where they were, but individuals might decide to move to another entity. We expected that too. We expected also some people who had already left to return. That's the natural course of things. After the Second World War, people went to Vojvodina and Slavonia and later came back home. So that possibility wasn't ruled out. But we reckoned that everybody would stay in their homes and would be given maximum protection so that they had no reason to go. I told you about that statement I made at the time, saying that we believed the Croats would take care of such minority populations in their area as we would take care of their minorities in our entity. That's a statement I made just before the war broke out. But our expectation was that the largest number of people would remain where they were with the exception of a small percentage of people who would leave, who would move.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I go to another piece of land? And the most convenient starting point on this one is to look at the Cutileiro map, to identify what I'm talking about. So if you could have that, we would be able to see this clearly enough on the screen. Do you see towards the top -- well it was towards the top of the screen it's just -- it's okay, it can stay where it is. Thank you, Madam Usher. Towards the top of the screen, it's about two-thirds of the way across. It's yes perhaps if you -- if you point, Mr. Krajisnik, yes come down a bit, I'm talking about that little blob of land which is Serb, marked Serb, coming down into -- it's a -- it's a -- that's it, that's it, we got it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, that is shown on Cutileiro map as Serb territory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's in the middle of -- well, it's not in the middle, it's within a much larger area of predominantly Muslim territory, as marked, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't drawn here as it was in the map, but as suggested by Mr. Cutileiro. There is about the area of Ozren, and maybe it would be worthwhile to explain this issue, because that's a good example of the misunderstandings and disagreements that we inherited from the previous system. I can show you on the first map where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will see that it's larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As far as the topic for discussion is concerned, you and I are I think going along the same lines here. If you -- if you then look at the -- P293, the complicated map, the one you've got in front of you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart says it's complicated and it's my favourite one. I don't know why he calls it complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If it's complicated, it's not necessarily bad, Mr. Krajisnik. If it's your favourite map, it's your favourite map.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sorry. This is this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's -- well, you've anticipated my question that identifies that and it's -- well, do you know off the cuff, Mr. Krajisnik, which municipality or municipalities it is within or straddles? We can work it out but you might just know immediately.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this area, after the war there was the Serb Municipality of Petrova. Around 100.000 Serbs lived there and then it was divided into five or six municipalities, this area, Sedrenik, Modrica, Doboj. I think Zepce. I think Lukavac as well, and in all those municipalities, Serbs were in the minority. And that was stigmatised as a Chetnik area and the Partizans during the war discriminated against this area. And we used to tell the negotiators, look at the size of this territory, they called it mountains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the beginning of your answer, you referred to the war. Did you refer to the Second World War or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Second World War. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, that's an example. And then, Mr. Cutileiro turned it into a smaller territory on his map because, and we later talked about it, he told us swap this with the Muslim segment up there on Cutileiro's plan and you will have linked up the eastern and the western part. Also, vis-a-vis the Croats, you see this blue area near Kupres, there was supposed to be a swap - it was discussed at one assembly session - against Croat areas in the corridor that we discussed. That was the subject of our talks in Graz. It was a geographical principal subject to agreement between the parties. If that was impossible to achieve then everything would remain as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm -- you're -- going to invite you to stay perhaps a little bit more slowly with my questions. You're jumping ahead and spreading around the map on matters with which you're familiar but I'd like to take it in bite-sized chunks, if I may. Staying with this piece of territory which we identified that Serb territory marked on the map, it appears to be at least just to the west of Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Srebrenik, I'm sorry. [Previous interpretation continues] ... old eyes. The -- and Your Honours will -- can see this conveniently on 211. The bigger map. It's where, of course, we have the municipalities more clearly marked, if one looks closely enough. The -- now, looking at - you don't like complicated map as the label - P293 the one with all the smaller bits of territory, P293, looking at that map, we can see very clearly that blue-marked area which -- yes, you're just putting the pointer on there. And Mr. Krajisnik, do you agree, and it's very apparent but I'll draw attention to it, that when we look at 211, we can see, can't we, that this is, if you like, a classic example of Serb majority territory in fact included entirely within municipalities where it's actually the Muslims who are in the majority in those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a good example from which you can see that there are several municipalities to each of these areas and you don't see any blue colour, unlike in the previous map. This area was divided into five or six municipalities. That's why this first complicated map is more precise, if you want to know what is located where in order to discuss. The same applies to Sarajevo and other places that were the subject of discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... going to bug us a little is the different colours on different maps. The -- on the bigger map, 211, the municipality map, blue is for Croats. On the P293, blue is for Serbs so we got to be a bit careful about colours, Mr. Krajisnik, otherwise it gets pretty complicated.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But here the Croats stole the blue from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- it's clearly the blob of land, if I can call it that, on the Cutileiro map that we have been talking about here is, as you mentioned a few minutes ago, it's distinctly smaller than the area of blue land on P293, within which it was contained, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's smaller, just like the other parts here that are not Serb are smaller. If you look at it, you will see that Mr. Cutileiro had a plan that he was going to use in giving us direction when we were identifying territories. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come to those other bits of land?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But your question was [indiscernible]. Mr. Stewart, could you ever have managed that Mr. Krajisnik would have said no, it's larger, it's bigger, and do you really think that this Court looking at this map, looking at those two features you've just drawn our attention to, that we would ever accept any owns other than it would be smaller?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's not really the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless we spent 50 lines on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not really the point of my question, and Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then if --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe, knows perfectly well that sometimes a question which Your Honour wishes to characterise as a stupid question in fact has its point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have included in the question that it -- this smaller portion and whatever you would like to draw our attention to it would have been sufficient. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you indicated that -- I believe you did a few minutes ago -- that it was at Mr. Cutileiro's initiative that there was a reduction of that area of land to what we see on Cutileiro map. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is more precise, this idea of Mr. Darwin, late Mr. Darwin, who was on the team of Mr. Cutileiro. He drew this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But is that right that the -- the instigation of the reduction of that area, that emanated from Cutileiro team rather than from the parties, did it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was -- was it a part of your thinking, the Bosnian Serb negotiators, that if you ended up with that smaller bit of land, that that would give the Serbs within that slightly wider area the opportunity, if you like, to withdraw into the core of that land, into what was provided by the Cutileiro map?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our position was that we should, whenever we can, ensure -- specifically with reference to this area, they wanted so badly to have their municipality, we were going to suggest that they should have an enclave within the federation, something similar to what others would have in our territory, because that is a very particular, very peculiar area, to which we were committed because those people suffered injustice for a long, long time. And they would have stayed up there. It's sort of plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was -- was it -- however, was it of special importance to you as the Bosnian Serb negotiators, that at least some part of that blue area of land that we see on P293 should become Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, as far as this territory was concerned, that it would be a subject for debate. We were interested in all the following talks as well, that this area remain within Republika Srpska, if I can put it that way. We were interested in that. Now, what would actually come through specifically, whether there would have been any exchanges, I cannot say, because this didn't happen in actual fact. Perhaps a different solution would have been found but I'm telling you what the aim was or what the plan was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, the -- apart from that, that particular piece of land that we've just been looking at, the only gap in the contiguity of Republika Srpska is the gap in the northeast, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You mean this part here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I do, indeed. Was that -- I called it a gap. It's as convenient a word as any. Was that gap the subject of specific discussion during the course of the Cutileiro talks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were discussions, and in one stage, that is to say in the second stage, when we saw this map, we wanted to find a solution, so that that constituent unit of ours would be linked up, if I can put it that way. I can tell you about all the combinations that were there to link this up, if we only talked to the Croats or if we involved the Muslim side too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When the agreement was reached -- I'm avoiding the word signed or concluded, Mr. Krajisnik, we already know that it was a little up in the air. But when the agreement was reached with this map annexed to it, how happy or unhappy were you, the Bosnian Serbs, with the result as seen on this map?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to ask kindly for a small correction. For us, this meant carrying out a deal: Recognise Bosnia, it will be transformed, give up Yugoslavia. Afterwards, regardless of whether somebody signed something or not, once we accepted Bosnia, for us it was an agreement, a final thing. And now, when you say whether we were happy or not, it's not only three or four negotiators that are making decisions. We democratically put this to the assembly and there was a wide discussion, there were many objections. If we were to discuss these objections and to rely on them, there would be a mixed feeling because expectations were higher. Everybody looked at things at a local level. If I can talk about the negotiators, once we had crossed the Rubicon and said that Bosnia was a state, through talks we saw that it wasn't easy for the other side either. So we had nevertheless a dose of satisfaction thinking well it's not bad and if it's not bad it's good. But it wasn't that we were elated. Or happy. Quite simply we said, if this is a solution, it's better for us to accept that and to put a stop to the crisis rather than embark on some kind of adventure, heaven forbid that a war break out. The negotiators wanted this to be accepted, and the assembly later adopted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If -- bearing in mind what you said in that answer, Mr. Krajisnik, if you had been asked at that time, when this map came to be annexed to the Cutileiro agreement, for your top three preferred improvements to this map for the Bosnian Serbs, what would they have been? I don't -- obviously, Mr. Krajisnik, we are not talking about colour the whole map blue for Serbs. You understand we are not talking about something as extreme as that. We are talking about your top three proposals that would have at least been within a sensible range to discuss across the table.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't explain the agreement we reached with the Croats so perhaps this answer will be insufficiently clear. My wish was for us to find a solution for that corridor in Posavina. That is one thing. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Use the pointer, Mr. Krajisnik, for that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think where the Posavina corridor is supposed to be is perfectly clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Posavina corridor, to carry out a transformation of Sarajevo in the future, that it should now be under the UN. And thirdly, I don't know if I'll be able to show it here, I beg your pardon. You see this here, this is Bosnia and Herzegovina's outlet to the sea, that is Neum, we wanted to have access to the sea either there or here, above Dubrovnik, a belt of land that should be given to the Croat side so that they would have access to the sea in this area where Prevlaka is and the border with Montenegro. To my mind, those were the three things that could have been resolved easiest of all. Two things were already there, almost. It's only the Posavina corridor that required further efforts. As for linking up territories along the Drina, the wish was to have some territories exchanged there in order to link up this corridor which we called our strategic objective but at that moment it wasn't the most important thing for me. The most important were the three that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said important for you. Did that reflect the importance for the negotiating team as a group or were there some differences?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, well, there is a map that we had proposed. It's a bit different from this map. Roughly, well, other negotiators too, I think -- well, deputies as well, put that corridor to the forefront, linking up the eastern and the western parts, that is to say linking up Krajina and Semberija. That was the most important. You see here, Sarajevo was treated separately, and it would have been under the UN. See, down here. So this is the Muslim part, the Croat part and the Serb part respectively, whereas Sarajevo is separate. That's this part here. It would have remained temporarily under the UN and then resolved later. That was also in the proposal of the Serb side. We agreed on that and we drew that. The Muslim side did not draw that but they put it into their own entity. All of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what I was -- what I was getting at was this. You agree in negotiations among, say, three teams, there are often going to be some pre-negotiations among the individual teams about what position should be adopted and so on. I'm simply asking whether the preferences that you had expressed as your own, whether there was any significant private difference of view and preferences within the team of you, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we were united. Maybe there were minor negligible differences between us but on principle, we were completely united on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the proposals in relation to the two pieces of land marked on the Cutileiro map within that very large swathe of Serb-marked territory in the northwest. So further up but right up in the northwest, that very, very large swathe -- or relatively very, very large, those two pieces of land there, one of which is marked Croat territory, the one to the east and the other partly Croat and partly Muslim, did those proposals present significant difficulties for you, the Bosnian Serb negotiating team?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Simply speaking, the intermediaries, that is the European Community, roughly identified where various ethnic areas lay, and they said if somebody wants to change something, it can only be done through bilateral agreements amongst you, about enclaves, et cetera. We didn't go for it because it required agreement and they too had certain demands. They were going to say what their priorities were. We were going to identify our priorities and then we were going to look for a solution. You have to -- it's much easier to work on the basis of a proposal than to put forward your demands without any underlying paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can we go back to the -- just put the maps on one side for the moment, please. Go back to the 8th assembly session? I want to go to page 47 of my version of the English. It should be page 59 in your version in your own language.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that number 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And it's Mr. Karadzic speaking again. He says -- do you see there is a reference to Mr. Jaksic in the middle of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So he says, "Some of -- in that sentence, some of those people are not even party members and the case -- as in the case of" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 46?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Page 46, it seems, in Your Honours' copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The reference to -- yes, Mr. Jaksic, "for instance, so let us not give him the licence to undermine our strategic commitment and objectives or to question our tactics. We are not changing our strategy. It remains the same. One state for Serbia or a federation of states and we will adjust the tactics to the conditions set down by Europe and we will seize at any opportunity that Europe presents us with or any concessions it makes and that's what we will do too." So is it again right, Mr. Krajisnik, that what Mr. Karadzic is saying there is not -- is not exactly fitting what you and he and Mr. Koljevic are prepared to discuss and consider in the course of the Cutileiro talks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Dusko Jaksic was the director of the economic institute, the institute of economy, and I think he's still in Banja Luka today. He made a feasibility study for the autonomous region of Krajina and he worked on - how shall I put it? - the rounding off of the Krajina territory. You can also find it in the press, that he came out with this feasibility study when the Autonomous Region of Krajina was included. He didn't offer other Serb areas because he thought that SAO Krajina should also be linked up, the SAO Krajina from Croatia. I don't know precisely what the underlying reason for this is but the old theory cropped up recurrently. We have Cutileiro negotiations, we have the Serb unit, and some people were going back to some superseded stages of regionalisation. That objection was frequently made against us, that we were talking about Krajina as a federal unit of Yugoslavia. Karadzic is saying here, however, we are not letting go of our strategic goals, and if Europe hands us something, we will take it. But we cannot look to satisfy those of our wishes which are unrealistic. Whereas this man, Jaksic took a regional view of things. He wasn't thinking broadly enough. So Karadzic criticised him for that. It didn't have any serious consequences, although we were trying to put a stop to any talk to -- about regionalisation, et cetera, and we had discussions and tried to persuade people and deputies from Krajina. There was one discussion between Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Jaksic dealing precisely with this topic. It was produced here, where Mr. Koljevic was trying to explain to him that this idea was not good, that the other version was better, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we turn on, please, to contribution of Mr. Zekic, which will be after point 14? It will be about a page or a bit more than a page after that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have number 14, but -- that's Mr. Kupresanin speaking, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Kupresanin. It's -- not sure the speakers are clearly identified in your copy at this point, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekic's excerpt. We found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your version, Mr. Krajisnik, it's in the middle of page 74, there is a sentence that says ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think the page is 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zekic starts speaking at the bottom of page 72 and continues on page --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. It's the middle paragraph on page 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He says, "I think that no agreement ..." There is no number against it. "I think that no agreement will be reached on Thursday." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, he says, "I think that no agreement will be reached on Thursday. For our part we would accept it but the Muslims won't. They won't. They would accept it only on condition that we make further concessions but we have no reason to do so. We have no reason to preserve any kind of a Bosnia and Herzegovina. If we can do nothing else, we can totally destroy and shatter it, and that is our task because if our state, Yugoslavia, was destroyed, we shall destroy this Bosnia with all the means available. Applause." Well, my question is really this, Mr. Krajisnik. Was that at the time -- was that as belligerent as it appears in the text?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It didn't sound belligerent, because we knew Mr. Zekic. Mr. Zekic was - how should I put this? - a man who would get cross easily and he was very brave. That's the way he behaved too. He went to Srebrenica on his own and he was killed from an ambush, as an MP. So he is putting this in epic terms. He is saying, "Why do we need Bosnia if we lost Yugoslavia?" On the one hand, he is undermining what we had said before and on the other hand he's saying the Muslims are not going to accept that. We would have accepted it. So he's mixing apples and oranges. Now, what he's saying we shall destroy, shatter. You can see what the atmosphere was like after the referendum of the Muslims and after they opted for an independent Bosnia, and now he is saying, Are you being realistic? The Muslims are not going to accept that, because they have already chosen the direction they want to take. There were others who made statements to that effect too. You will see the next speaker after him, Kupresanin. I don't know who he said but that is the way these people speak, in epic terms, and then they are applauded and then the chairman has to try to calm things down and channel things into a realistic discussion. Their type of discussion is more popular than people who say, wait a minute, we have to do things differently. But it's not realistic. It's realistic conclusions that are ultimately drawn, not the kind that Mr. Zekic proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can you find the bottom paragraph on page 74 of your -- sorry, it's 71. There has been a hitch with the scanning. It's 71 of your document. But it's out -- it may be immediately before page 75. It may have got out of order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was out of order but it could just be put in the right place because the page is missing there, 71.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the paragraph starting, "I suggest that Karadzic, Koljevic, and Krajisnik," which is on page 57 of my English version. Do you see that? "I suggest that Karadzic, Koljevic, and Krajisnik." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 71? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's number 14, where number 14 is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: English page 56 for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It appears to be Mr. Kalinic speaking, and he says, I'd suggest that Karadzic, Koljevic, and Krajisnik merely initial the documents the gentlemen agree on, if it's suitable for us. If we agree, we can verify the document at this assembly on Friday. This means that we extend our full confidence to our negotiators but the document cannot be approved without our participation, and Mr. Cutileiro should be told that they are only negotiators on behalf of the Serbian Assembly and that the Serbian Assembly alone can approve the signing (applause). Was that the attitude that you expected the assembly to adopt?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we expected that, and that was our intention, that the negotiations be supported. Mr. Kalinic is being helpful here in saying, well, he is not saying, maybe I made a mistake. Maybe the translation is a bit wrong because it's sort of a free interpretation by the translator. He doesn't say "only." "The authority given to us is only to initial a document not to adopt it. And then the assembly will adopt the document." That is what is written here. So, of course, well, the majority was in favour of that so there was applause here too. Like in other places. So we would be authorised to initial it possibly but then the assembly would discuss this, adopt it, ratify it and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But it didn't surprise you that this was the position that the assembly adopted in relation to your authority?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. It didn't surprise me because we couldn't do anything and we didn't want to do anything and we were not authorised to accept something without the assembly giving their approval. We wanted things to be as legitimate as possible. Ultimately none of us -- the negotiators had the right to do things apart from the assembly and we kept going back to the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This would be a suitable moment for a break. We'll have a break until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you speak at this same assembly meeting that we are looking at, at page 77, which is page 62 in the English version I'm looking at. Can you find that, Mr. Krajisnik? It's margin number 16.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You comment and I'm not going to go into that again. You comment on what Mr. Kupresanin has said. I won't go through that in detail. It's the point we considered earlier. Then you say about five paragraphs on, "I'm sorry but if you say quotes if Banja Luka is not the capital of Serbian Krajina." [as read] Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "If Banja Luka is not the captain of Serbian Krajina, it doesn't become that. I can say here irrespective of who is present, that the capital of the Serbian people can be one city and one city alone, Belgrade. This attempt to impose Banja Luka, you can put it forward and embellish it but I want to tell you gentlemen that individuals who are not part of your ethnic group nor are they members of Serbian Democratic Party, have the main word in Krajina. I say this before God and the people here, whether you like it or not, and what is happening in Krajina is the division of the Serbian people which they have no right to provoke in Krajina." I want to read together with this, Mr. Krajisnik, the very last paragraph of this particular contribution of yours, before Mr. -- you hand over the floor to Mr. Kupresanin. So if you just turn to the very end of that speech, you say, "We have the opportunity to preserve the Serbian people in a single state, to preserve the entire Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and have it become part of the Serbian empire. I wouldn't have a clear conscience to approve the words of anyone here from this position and place. I have to say what I've said." Did any concept of Serbian empire with Belgrade as its capital form part of the policy of the SDS leadership at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'll explain what I meant by this. This is a defence mechanism against the conclusion adopted by the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I said that Belgrade was a centre, meaning a spiritual centre for the Serbian people. If I had said Sarajevo, they would have replied that it was a Muslim town. So it couldn't be the Serbian centre. The issue was whether we were going to choose Banja Luka or Sarajevo as the capital of our constituent unit. As for the empire, it's obvious that I borrowed their style of speech, trying to answer in the same vein and discourage them for what they thought was imperative for the Autonomous Region of Krajina and Mr. Vojo Kupresanin later explained what it was all about. The conclusions of the Autonomous Region of Krajina were very dangerous indeed, something like an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then if we just go back a few paragraphs in that same speech, about one, two, three, four, five paragraphs, you say, "Gentlemen" -- it's four, I think, "Gentlemen, we want to remain in a single state." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Gentlemen we want to remain in a single state together with Serbia, Montenegro, the independent Autonomous Region of Krajina, now the Krajina state, and the rest. We just need to agree on the method to achieve this. If we don't want to do this by certain methods, let us put a stop to it. You know what our profession has always been, to wage war." Was there a point that you were trying to get across to the deputies by that particular remark?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very easy to understand in the Serbian language. I replied to those who were against the results achieved in the negotiations, within the framework of the Lisbon Conference of the time, and I told them if you don't want to pursue this method, if you want a state for Krajina instead, then let's put a full stop to this and see what the alternative is. The alternative is war. And I meant the people of Krajina whose historic vocation was to be soldiers, because they were defenders of the border, and I was saying practically are we now supposed to go back and do something that we all know would end in very bad consequences? And they were all taken aback because my tone was very different to my usual tone. I borrowed their tone and I borrowed their rhetoric. Maybe in your language it sounds like we have two options, one is peace the other is war. I am suggesting a different way of looking at it. I wasn't calling on anybody to make war. I was saying that we should work for peace, whereas war is something that requires no work. Anybody can do that. Anybody can understand what is written here in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- there are, as there have been with previous -- there are a number of intercepts relating to the period which comes up to the end of February 1992, which is where we are now. In the usual way, Your Honour, may I invite Mr. Josse to deal with those with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the bundle are with Mr. Haider. Could one be given to the witness, please? My learned friends in the Prosecution have one. The first intercept in this bundle is one that we -- Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic. It's dated the 26th of December 1991. Your Honours, by our records, this has two exhibit numbers, it's part of P154, part of 389 as well. It was played at page 8079 to 8088 of the transcript. I don't intend to have it replayed. On the first page, we see a reference to the fact that Mr. Krajisnik says that he was down in Novi Grad until late.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that's what I want to ask you about initially, Mr. Krajisnik. Why had you gone there on the 26th of December?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I visited Novi Grad perhaps a few times. That's the municipality where I used to reside. I was on the initiative board of the Serbian Democratic Party there a month before the elections, and in a way I had some private reasons for going there too. I don't know whether it was a private reason that took me there this time, but that private reason that I had later turned into a business reason. President of that municipality, Mr. Ismet Cengic, testified here. I asked him to receive me and to help me about legalising the status of my house. He did so and he helped me, but I also attended the Municipal Board of the SDS of Novi Grad. Or maybe they invited me, I'm not sure any more. And after I left, some disagreements occurred between the two factions that I told you about when I spoke about the first time I went there and was appointed to the initiative board of the SDS in that municipality. So I know I went there concerning some business that had to do with my house, but maybe I also attended the board, and upon my return, maybe I reported about the situation from that original board in that town, from which I became a candidate of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A little further down, there is a reference by you to that man, Unkovic, contributed a lot to that but there were others there as well. What are you alluding to when you mention Mr. Unkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Unkovic, you remember I spoke about him earlier, he was a candidate number 1 for a MP from our municipality and I was candidate number 2. I think he took over from me later. Either as president of the Municipal Board or maybe that inner circle. On one occasion, when they were making some staffing decisions I suggested to Mr. Karadzic to correct this injustice and to appoint him minister for culture. But that was rejected. They rejected it. I wanted him to have a posting of that sort because I felt guilty because in the end I got the appointment although he had been number 1. He belonged to one group and those who were opposed were on -- in the other group, and I was trying to say that he was not alone in causing that conflict. There were others too on the Municipal Board who contributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The second part of this intercept is really a description by Mr. Karadzic to you of negotiations that he is involved in. In the English, towards the top of page 3, he introduces the subject by saying, helpfully, "On another topic, there is a small disappointment you will understand me. It appears that Milosevic, he went today to Macedonia. It seems that he immediate a step in the direction of Izetbegovic-Gligorov platform." What can you tell the Trial Chamber about that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point in the negotiations between presidents of republics, an initiative was plead by late Mr. Izetbegovic from Bosnia, therefore, and the president of Macedonia, Gligorov, and it was called platform Izetbegovic-Gligorov. It envisaged a solution whereby the republics, the former republics, would be linked doubly. Bosnia would have closer ties, formal ties, federal ties, whereas Macedonia and Slovenia would have looser, confederal ties, and that's what Mr. Karadzic is referring to, namely that late president Milosevic had come closer to that option and was -- or appeared ready to accept it, and he later did accept it in Sarajevo. However, it was ultimately rejected by Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to read you back in English a little bit of what you've just said and ask you if you can confirm whether it's right. If reads in English, "Bosnia would have closer ties, formal ties, federal ties, whereas Macedonia and Slavonia [as read] would have looser confederal ties and that's what Mr. Karadzic is referring to." Did you just say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, but the read back should have said Slovenia and not Slavonia and that may be a source of some confusion for Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do he need me to read that again, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I understand. Maybe it's a slip of the tongue but what I said was that Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina would have firmer ties, whereas Slovenia and Croatia would have confederal ties, looser ties. That's what I meant. Maybe I made a slip of the tongue. I don't think I did actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't think it was a slip of the tongue. That's why I asked you the question. Thank you. I'd like to move on, please, to the next intercept in the bundle. That is one on New Years' Day 1992 between you and Mr. Karadzic again. It bears four numbers by our record, 64, 67, 292, and 403. Again according to our research it's been played in full twice to the Chamber, once on the 24th of February 2004 at 1529, where it wasn't transcribed, Your Honour, and again at 8325 where it was transcribed, initially in the evidence of Mr. Treanor and then in the evidence of Mr. Bijelica. I'm not going to invite it to be played for a third time. I would like to take you to quite a long passage, page 4 at the very bottom in English. Again, I'll read it slowly and I'm sure you'll find the place when the translator picks it up. And Karadzic says, "She shouldn't have, fuck her. Fuck her, I was just reading this Izetbegovic interview. Krajisnik: Yeah, what's it like."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please just find it? Could you just wait for a second? 0530? Just a moment, please, yes. Yes. I found the page. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll go on. "Karadzic: Well he's crazy, man. He is directly irritating the Serbs. Krajisnik: Yeah? Karadzic: He was like, if we are all the same, this and that and a sovereign and independent Bosnia, now he's talking openly of a sovereign and independent Bosnia. Does he want someone to destroy Sarajevo? Krajisnik: Yeah. Karadzic: Fuck, he's really crazy. He now openly talks of a sovereign and independent Bosnia. Krajisnik: Yeah. Karadzic: You know that. Krajisnik: Yeah. Karadzic: It was until recently -- fuck him we will release our tigers and let them do their job. Krajisnik: Yeah, can you imagine this impertinence. Karadzic: Fuck. I -- we've been calming the Serb people for a year because of his foolishness. What can I do? I will not be calming anyone anymore, nor can I. Krajisnik: Nobody says we don't want -- this isn't an independent, that's not a state. He says it's a -- sovereign so it's equal in the talks. Now he says independent. Fucking they really are crazy. Europe is crazy too if they think this can be so. Man, this is impossible, this. I don't think there is a man who could turn the situation around and now make it so." I'll stop there if I may. This is clearly a reference to something Mr. Izetbegovic has said. What was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was an interview here that was there as a document of Mr. Izetbegovic. I think it was his New Years' interview, and that is the occasion. In our discussions about declarations and memorandums, the response coming from the other side was we don't want an independent Bosnia without the approval of all. We just want Bosnia to be sovereign, like all the rest, equitable. It is sovereign because that's what the constitution says. It's a sovereign republic but within Yugoslavia. Now, in that article, he says we want independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, preparing for the referendum and so on. Now, this is Mr. Karadzic's anger, and he is using various unrealistic words here, that he's going to release some radical elements of his that he kept under control and so on. However, there is one thing that is true and realistic in what Mr. Karadzic says. All the time the Serbs were being persuaded to go for negotiations to find an agreement, a solution, that there would be no unilateral solutions and that the Muslim side would not ask for independence because that is dangerous, without agreeing on what a transformed Bosnia would be like. Please, there is a statement made by Mr. Karadzic on the 17th of January. He says, "No division, not a -- not a division but a transformation of Bosnia-Herzegovina." So after our declaration on the Serb republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he said we want transformation not a division. That is a consequence of that interview, as far as I can remember, that interview given by Mr. Izetbegovic. It was the first time that he used the word independence, not sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Any idea what Mr. Karadzic is referring to when he says, "We will release our tigers and let them do their job"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He meant nothing. It's just an expression of powerlessness. "Release our tigers." There are no tigers. It's something that -- well, in our part of the world, if you say something like if you don't bring me that notebook tomorrow, I'll kill you. It's sort of rhetorical. Then also there is this saying he's asleep as if he were slaughtered or something like that. And he meant I'm not going to keep my people that way any longer, let them do what they want. There are no tigers. Wars are different but this is the 1st of January. He's speaking out of fear because he knows what it means. That's what my view is. That's why I kept trying to pacify things. In a way I tried to calm his terrible dissatisfaction down, his terrible dissatisfaction over Mr. Izetbegovic's interview. And I agreed with him because it was not a good interview and at that time it was not a fair interview on the part of the late Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this interview, in this intercept, later Mr. Karadzic is saying in English, "No way to release us. People, we should hold them back." So what exactly does this mean for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's what he meant. At the assembly, and at all gatherings we kept saying that there would be no war, that we would reach agreement and so on. You saw those previous sessions, how much persuasion there was there to channel things towards a solution as sought by the European Community, and now he said well we are just going to let go and let everybody do whatever they want and then they will see. So it's a sign of powerlessness well not of powerlessness but of anger. It's not that he can release anybody or anything. He can't even talk them into doing something serious. This is rhetorical. This is a rhetoric that is readily understood in our parts. Well, rhetoric that is perhaps not understandable in other parts of the world but it's understandable in our parts, that you say something in anger that is not exactly very balanced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent there might have been confusion of what I read on the transcript because it does not reflect the text you read, since the text says, Karadzic, Radovan saying, "No way, we need to release those people. We shouldn't hold them back," whereas the transcript now reads, we should hold them back. But the portion of the intercepted telephone conversation says, "they -- we should not hold them back." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I've understood that, of course, it's rhetoric when you say "We will release our tigers." [In English] "And let them do their job." [Interpretation] But a bit later, I found an expression that was more explicit, we need to release those people, we should not hold them back. So excuse me if I may continue. So, as a reader, when I read this, it seems as if Mr. Karadzic wanted to say that there were people who were ready to really go right at it, that it wouldn't be possible to always hold them back, you know, in front of provocation, and you're not interpreting it in the same way as I am, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry. I cannot see this or what is this, impertinence? I can't find what you read out just now. Perhaps the interpreters can help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we'll find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I found it now, yes. No, no. This is the meaning of what I said. I said that we don't have to release them. It's not that we have to approve that. No way. They are going to do that on their own, like it or not. What I was trying to say was, well, he said we are going to release them. We will let them or whatever. I was saying, well, you don't have to let them. They will -- well, they will do it spontaneously on their own. There will be chaos. So this is an answer from me. And then he continues and says, "Well, you cannot stop them any longer." So he's giving me an answer, not preventing something, stopping someone from doing something. He is saying as if he could stop someone from doing something, and then I'm saying, no way, what does this mean? Well, I appreciate -- this is something that was not defined properly because this answer doesn't make any sense when we read all of it, but, well, in that sense, it follows what Karadzic said, "No way, what does that mean, really? I appreciate the nation, you," meaning the Muslims, "Yugoslavs, you know, they started something and they have some idea as well, but I put this mildly. They want me to help them in the parliament so they can get the status of a constituent people." This is something that has nothing to do with the previous thing that was said. Probably some party of Yugoslavs asked for something in the parliament but that has nothing to do with the first thing that Mr. Karadzic was saying. Somehow -- well, that's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There may be one small translation issue that's been brought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, on your page, 0322-0531, could you read the very first two lines of that page, which is a comment from Mr. Karadzic. Read it slowly so that it can be translated again.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "No way. We have to let people -- we don't or we should not fuck around with them." Well, the style is not very good either, if those are the two lines you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour it was brought to my attention that in the present translation, the use of the word "those" is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have even more differences now because on paper it reads, "No way, we need to release those people," whereas it now says, "We have to let people," and then "We shouldn't hold them back. Now has become -- we don't or we should not fuck around with them," which is not exactly the same. Could I ask CLSS to verify the translation specifically on these two lines, because the language as translated on paper now is more suggestive than the language as translated now orally. I see some of the -- one of the interpreters raising his hand or -- no. Could we -- perhaps, Mr. Registrar, you could try to be in touch with CLSS to have this verified; very specifically, these two lines. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik in fact I was going to move on to the next intercept in this mini bundle. That is one on an unspecified date in January between yourself and Mr. Karadzic. It's -- it bears two numbers, it's been played at 1554 of the transcript, but not transcribed, again during the evidence of Mr. Treanor. And on the first page, we see that you are asking about the position on the referendum. You then discuss that further with Mr. Karadzic, and you say, on page 3 in the English, and I'll read this slowly again whilst the place is found, "Listen, what I had in mind, I think we have to say publicly we consider this referendum, it's a referendum. Karadzic: National? Krajisnik: Yes, of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. There was a reference to page 3 in the English. We went to the next intercept sequentially in the materials provided. That contains 2 pages of English translation so perhaps an ERN will be necessary to point us towards the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, the ERN in translation is 02079370, 02079371 -- I look at it I can see that there is going to be a problem because it says draft translation. I suspect that there is a revised translation for the actual exhibit and I'm afraid I don't have that. Is that the difficulty? I don't know whether my learned friend can assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, I'm reasonably confident I have the translation that was actually exhibited. I'm happy to provide it to the Registrar to pass it along so that we can move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Am I getting that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps put it on the ELMO and then have it enlarged such that everyone can read it, and it would here be on -- just trying to find the relevant portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact I was looking for -- it's at 10, the press conference, yes, in the one it's in numbers and the other it's in -- written out. For you, Mr. Krajisnik in the B/C/S version it's two-thirds down on page 1, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll read on, if I may. In fact, perhaps the usher could pull --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could it be zoomed in a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to say scrolled up, in fact, because with it in front of us -- the other way, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it should not be scrolled up too much, I would say, because you started on the line -- well, which is now in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I know I did, Your Honour, but since it's there I'm not going to read those few lines out because iz the next substantive answer for Mr. Krajisnik -- over the page, please, Madam Usher -- that I would like to direct Mr. Krajisnik to in reality. There it is. It's this. "Where they didn't help us we have no reasons to help them but we won't hinder it. In any case, we'll greet it. It would be good to say. As for the official organs, they are not obliged to do because this was brought by one unofficial meeting and not official. Yes, yes, and we won't give up ourselves. Up by that date certain things will become crystallised and that conditions set by the HDZ will be fulfilled, that we will with such an agreed standpoint in that case probably when all those things are resolved, it won't be disputable even for Serbs to get out, you know." What are you saying about the referendum, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, a small correction. What is it says here is "we are holding on," but logically, it would be "we hope," not [B/C/S spoken] but [B/C/S spoken], that things will be crystallised by that date. So it is not [B/C/S spoken] but [B/C/S spoken]. It's rather similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The provisional translation seems to be clearer on that matter than the final one, but ... Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, this was probably after the 25th of January, the 27th of January 1992, a conversation taking place then, when the Muslim and the Croat sides -- or rather, there was a meeting of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I actually persuaded the MPs of the Serb Democratic Party or rather our club that they go and attend this joint session. That is to say on the 27th. I think it was the 27th of January. Then a big, profound debate took place there. It's a historic session, if I can call it that, and we were so close to a solution there that the Muslim side even agreed. And there is a video clip here where Mr. Cengic and Mr. Karadzic are at the rostrum together and at the last moment, actually, the late Mr. Izetbegovic cancelled this so this idea went down the drain. Then we, the Serb side, vetoed this and we provided these 20 signatures and asked this to be referred to the Council for National Security. That is why this is irregular. When I say this, we are saying that this is a plebiscite or a referendum of two peoples, not Bosnia-Herzegovina for us, so what I'm saying here is that we should not hinder them, we should welcome this if we look at it that way and if they helped us in any way when we had a plebiscite they should be helped too. Our official organs are not duty bound to help, in our view, but they should not hinder it either. And Mr. Karadzic agrees with that. The referendum of the Muslims and Croats is something that we thought we should not hinder but that an official statement should be made. You have a letter from Mr. Radojko from Petrovac he's the one who signed it asking for instructions and that is why we were duty bound to make some kind of statement. Mr. Karadzic is saying here, "I will say that at the press conference" and I'm saying if by some date conditions have been met perhaps we will go for a referendum too, which was a sensitive issue. So that was the meaning, that we should not hinder this referendum. Because they did not hinder our plebiscite either when we held it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I don't know whether this was your last question already on the matter but since I have a to announce a few procedural matters as well with the indulgence of the technicians and the interpreters, I would rather then invite you to do that next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course. Could I just say this? I would invite the Chamber to allow Mr. Krajisnik to take this mini bundle away with him? Even though he was notified yesterday of these intercepts, there seems no reason why he can't have that bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Krajisnik, you may take the bundle with you and further read it over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me just confirm my understanding that the bundle we are talking about is the listing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The intercept bundle, I take it, just intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The intercept bundle that he has in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber would like to address a few matters. First, the claim would like to deal with a few matters related to items in evidence or to be tendered by the parties. With respect to P529, tab 408, the parties agreed to modify the translation of an intercept dated the 20th of June 1992. The portion reads, and I quote, "Well, I'm chasing those pigs up there, these Muslims that left these pigs behind. Two to three days I've been doing that." The words "these Muslims" should deleted and replaced with "those Bosniaks (or Bosniak family)". The claim requests the Registrar to modify and initial the translation accordingly with a reference to today's transcript. The claim would also like the OTP to tender immediately the translations for P1077, P1079, P1081, and P1082, and P1084. But since Mr. Registrar showed me just before we entered into court a bundle of documents, I take it that most of it, of the list I just gave, is covered by what has just been submitted by the Prosecution. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with the exception of 1081. Let me explain the situation with 1081. 1080 was an interview with Mr. Poplasen. 1080 was in B/C/S, it was then translated into English. That became Exhibit 1080.1. The identical interview in English was 1081. We have not translated 1081 because it's the identical interview that is found in 1080.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it, Mr Josse, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon had previously explained that to me. I, of course, would like to look at the translation that have just been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've got until next Tuesday to raise any objections, if that -- is that enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine. That is enough so long as they are given to me this afternoon, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then that leaves 1077, 79, 82, and 84 are submitted and you have for these exhibits as well one week from today to raise any objections as we usually give you, to these translations, failing which all of these items I just mentioned to the exclusion of the one, 1081, will be automatically admitted into evidence. And then you'll get for 1081 a week as well, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then with respect to 1092 and 1092A, which is a Tanjug news report and video clip, on the 21st of March the Chamber asked the OTP to submit the video, the English transcript and the B/C/S transcript by the 5th of April. The Chamber requests the Prosecution to tender these items at the first opportunity. The Defence will then have one week to object. In the absence of any objection the items will be admitted into evidence without further action by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have those, Your Honour. Trying to locate those and if not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll provide them to the Registrar and to Mr. Josse this afternoon --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll file them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that they are now tendered. We were informed that items P851, P853, P854, were not properly identified on the exhibits list. Moreover, the corresponding B/C/S transcripts have not been provided. The Chamber requests the Registrar to modify the titles of the exhibits on the list to better reflect their content. Also the Chamber notes that since the translation of exhibits into B/C/S from one -- into B/C/S from one of the official languages of the Tribunal is for the benefit much the Defence, there is no need to have a B/C/S translation if the Defence does not request one and that's for P-exhibits or does not arrange for one to be made and that, of course, would apply for Defence exhibits. The Chamber further requests the Prosecution to file as soon as possible the photographic material on the destruction of buildings in 1992 and the exemplars of contracts related to the forced surrender of property. There must be plenty of photographs or film frames shot in 1992 on which the effects of the armed conflict were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that project is sitting on my desk, at least the preliminary project is sitting on my desk. This is a -- the situation that arises. We can identify destruction that took place in 1992. The photographs, however, were taken subsequent to 1992. The Court order says it requires us to produce photographs taken in 1992. So we can tie destruction that occurred in 1992 through witnesses' testimony. We can cite to the testimony. But often times we weren't on the scene and didn't have access to the scene when the destruction occurred or shortly even after the destruction occurred. So a lot of our pictures are taken in 2000, 2002, maybe 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could discuss the matter with the Defence, whether the Defence would have any doubt as to whether the destruction was caused in 1992. I'm not talking about reason or the causes of destruction. We are just images to get a better impression and even though the pictures may have been taken at a later stage. And then we would like to receive it as soon as possible. Then I -- that should not refrain you from presenting the contracts, Mr. Harmon. And I know how it is. If there is a project on your desk you would like to get it off it as soon as possible. Then with respect to item D139, the missing compact disk was tendered on the 27th of April and the item is therefore admitted into evidence now. With respect to item D146, the English translation was tendered on the 26th of April and the item is therefore admitted into evidence. All of the items tendered during the examination of Witness Bijelica were admitted by the decision of the 24th of April. However, two of these exhibits, namely D162 G and D163 still lack English translations. In addition, the Defence has not yet submitted the compact disk of D161, a video which was played in court. These three exhibits are therefore only provisionally admitted. The Defence is requested to provide the compact disk of item D161, as soon as possible, and to submit the missing English translation, translations related to items used during the examination and Mr. Bijelica within two weeks. These items will be admitted without more upon receipt of the required translations and the compact disk. The Chamber finally reminds the Defence that the deadline for objections by the Defence to the Nielsen source material submitted on the 25th of April by the OTP expires on the 9th of May. This concludes the Chamber's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just -- Your Honour, since it got a reference, I with Mr. Zahar's permission handed to Mr. Krajisnik earlier an unmarked copy of P853.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To say that I immediately would know what P853 is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's an interview with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then at least now the OTP is informed about it. Then I wish everyone a good weekend. We adjourn until next Monday, but not, Mr. Krajisnik, until after I've instructed you not to speak with anyone about the testimony given or still to be given. Adjournment until next Monday, Mr. Registrar, we are sitting, I think in the afternoon or is that a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In the afternoon, Your Honours, in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will be quarter past 2, same courtroom.
